utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue the examination of witnesses, I had a look at the schedule that had been given to the Defence, what witnesses would be called, and finally, this Chamber also got a copy of this letter. And it turned out that on this letter, now the time, the estimated time for the witnesses, is not indicated, so we have to find that somewhere in our files. So I think it would be better to have that as well. For that reason, and also in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding about what protective measures there are, what the time estimate is, whether everyone has got the copies disclosed to him, I tried to assist the parties, and I did it just for once. If Mr. Usher could please come and distribute this. I have enough copies, a couple of copies to the Prosecution and to the Defence. This is the information this Chamber would like to have at the beginning of each week. That means the names of the witnesses, exhibit numbers, of course to be described more in detail on a separate list, time estimates, protective measures granted. That's the Prosecution part. We want this list filled in, given by the Prosecution to the Defence so that the Defence checks whether there are any exhibits not yet disclosed or whether there's any problem as far as the language is concerned, and similarly, whether there are any previous statements of the witness not yet disclosed. Please put your name on it, please put a date on it, and inform the Chamber so that we have got really everything we need to know. Of course, I would have expected this in one way or another to be organised by the parties themselves. The format of this can be provided by the Chamber, because it has been drafted by the Chamber, so you can -- it's really to assist you. And whenever there's any change in the order, exhibits or whatsoever, please make a new list, put a new date on it, give it to the Defence again, the Defence checks whether they have got everything they need, and then a copy to be given to the Chamber. This is actually the way it should have been organised, and I am assisting you now to organise this way. So this is just an example. I'll try to figure out the time estimates from the lists available to us. If it's not correct, please let me know, but this is what we could figure out as what we could expect over the next few days. If there's any problem already as far as this list is concerned, if it's not about Witness D, then the Defence may inform the Chamber during the day. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as Witness D is concerned, the Defence has received -- or rather, I handed over my learned friend from the Prosecution information that I have received, the map, so we do have that. I should like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence has a list of witnesses, enjoying a pseudonym as a protective measure, and Witness K, on my list, is the second witness. I should like to ask my learned colleagues if there has been a change in the order for witnesses with pseudonyms on that list, to inform the Defence on time so that we avoid misunderstanding. Because Witness K on my list of protected witnesses is witness 2. My colleagues informed me yesterday, or rather, on Saturday, that this particular witness, Witness K, is not the one that I thought he was, the name that we have, but that he is, in fact, a different person. I don't know if the Trial Chamber has been informed of this, and whether they have the pseudonyms with the corresponding names correctly listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope so. We'll see. Of course, it's -- as far as I remember, the list of pseudonyms was attached, I think, to the motion which the protective measures was sought. So that's what guides us at this moment. If this is not correct any more, then ... Mr. Ierace, has any --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, may I just add one more point: It was the list dated the 13th of December, 2001, which my colleagues faxed to me, the 13th of December. It is a list of witnesses enjoying protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could, please, both the Defence and the Prosecution approach the Bench with their list of names and pseudonyms of witnesses so we can check whether we all have the same. Compare it with my list. The thick one, is that from the Prosecution? And one sheet is from the Defence. Okay, let me just ... Yes, these lists are not the same, so we have to compare them in detail. Would you please do this during the next break, because you have different lists now. I see this one is faxed on the 13th of December, and this is one -- an annex to a motion filed on the 30th of October. So there is a French list, which is different and from a later date. And since I was also informed according to the list the Prosecution just provided, would you please sort it out and inform the Chamber which is the correct list. As far as I can see, Witness D, there's no problem, so we can start with Witness D. And then have to verify which is the true list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could I just make the comment that the list I have handed up is an annex to the motion that is the 30th of October last year. Initially, that was a confidential and ex parte motion. The ex parte status was lifted. So I don't understand why the Defence is confused as to the details of Witness K. But we will speak to them again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see is that there are different names connected to Witness K.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't know that both lists came from the Prosecution, the one that the Defence has handed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please compare these lists during the first break and see what the problem exactly is. And if there's no problem, I will be glad to hear so. Since there's no problem as far as Witness D is concerned, I suggest that Witness D is brought into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we will be able to extricate ourselves from the situation. As far as [redacted] the Prosecution has provided two translations and not one, but they are not identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did I hear you mention a name?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, be very careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry. I misspoke. It is a mistake on my part. I was speaking of Witness D. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, will you prepare what has to be done. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two translations, but we will make do with one of them, although they are not exactly the same. So one translation would be sufficient. I should like to thank the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One translation of what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's clear to me. So we now can proceed. Mr. Usher, could you please bring in the witness. May I remind the parties, to start with, the Prosecution, to put off their microphones immediately when the witness starts answering the question since voice distortion is linked to the microphone of the witness but, of course, the distance is rather short. And therefore, it might be possible that part of what he says can be heard by your microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome to this courtroom. Since a pseudonym has been granted to you, we will call you "Witness D." So that is you on from this moment. Now, Witness D, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration of which the text will be handed out to you by the usher. Would you please make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll first be examined by the Prosecution. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just in order to avoid any mistakes, in the earliest stage of your examination, a sheet will be given to you with your name on it, just answer the question put by the Prosecution to you, but do not read your name aloud. Just say, according to what is asked to you, yes or no. Because if you would read your own name, then the whole protective measures would not be effective any more. Mr. Ierace, you're going to examine the witness? Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the sheet be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please look at the details on the sheet of paper in front of you. And please do not read them out, but can you confirm that the details are correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. They cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's something wrong with the microphone, I think. Mr. Usher, could you please check whether the microphone is close enough to the witness and that it's -- or is it a matter of the voice distortion which causes the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's working now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the answer just given on the question by the Prosecution so that the interpreters can hear you and can translate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, what it says on the piece of paper is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think for technical reasons we just -- the name sheet has been tendered into evidence, sealed, and is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3646, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, whereabouts were you born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until 1992, had you lived anywhere else apart from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it, therefore, you went to school in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you undertake any university studies in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you obtain a degree as a result of those studies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of degree was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was a law degree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some stage did you do military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that was in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us what year or years you did that service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: From October 1982 to September 1983.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At a later stage were you called up by some form of reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what period of time did you stay in the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Several weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now ask you some questions about the outbreak of hostilities in Sarajevo. When did that armed conflict commence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what district or municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The municipality of Novo Sarajevo, and the district was called Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, according to your observations, did military forces move into Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. My learned colleague -- I should like to ask my learned colleague to rephrase the question, because the witness mentioned no military forces, which was the term used in the question asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's not only that no military forces were yet mentioned, but no going into Grbavica as well. So would you please rephrase that question, since this might not -- an issue which is not uncontested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I had assumed that by now that was not a contested issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your observations, given that you were living in Grbavica on the 6th of April, 1992, are you able to tell us whether there were persons Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bearing arms in Grbavica at about that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In that part of Grbavica where I was, there weren't, not yet, not on the 6th of April, in the part where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any relevant observations in parts of Grbavica at around that time, other than where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Above Grbavica, armed people were stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to determine what group, if any, they were affiliated with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They were people who mostly lived there and who were given arms. Trenches had been dug there, and they were there with their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any activity at around that time -- I withdraw that. Did you notice whether there was any activity around that time, in that area, by the forces of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Before Grbavica was taken over, the JNA units, on several occasions, together with people from the SDS who had arms as well, went to Grbavica in the course of the night and would return before dawn to their original positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that pattern of behaviour continue beyond around the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. What I said took place after the 6th of April. That's when it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It happened from the 6th of April to mid-May, when Grbavica had been taken control of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that Grbavica had been taken control of in mid-May, what exactly happened at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The army, the JNA, and the people from the SDS who were armed took control of Grbavica, militarily speaking, and they set up the front line along the Miljacka River, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether there was a headquarters at that stage, that is, after Grbavica had been taken control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after Grbavica had been taken, the headquarters of those units present there had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown a map. A copy has been provided to the Defence. It is marked P3637. That exhibit number comprises five maps. This particular one has written at the top of it "Map 1."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, before the witness is shown this document, the Defence would like to point out that we are not talking about a map of the town here, but only a portion of a map. As I said, this is just a portion of a map, not a map in its entirety, just a copy thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we cannot refer to it as a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is a map, but a map of a part of the city, as far as I understand. Could it really create any confusion, especially if we put it on the ELMO? I don't think so. But you're quite right, it's a part of the city only, but it still is a map. Could it be put on the ELMO for further questioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you make a statement to an investigator from the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal in February of 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of making that statement, were you shown the map which is now before you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you something, Mr. Ierace. Do you intend to have this map also put on the ELMO? As I just asked, I didn't hear you oppose. Are you going to use it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please ask one of your team to stand next to the usher and take care that the name of the witness which appears on the map is not shown on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Ms. Harris will place a sticker over that part of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I will re-ask that question. When you made that statement, were you shown the original of the map which is before you now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make some markings on that map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do those appear before you now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate on that map approximately where you were living in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that marking which appears on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The location was marked by me with an X.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please point to that X on the map with your finger or with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said in evidence earlier this morning that before Grbavica was occupied, there were some forces that moved in above Grbavica. Did you indicate that position on the map in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you make that indication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I indicated that position with a black line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please point to the black line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That line appears to run on the southern side of a road. How is that road known? How was it known then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The road is commonly referred to as Transit, or a bypass actually. It runs on the southern side of this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said this morning that that line was above Grbavica. Having regard to that evidence, did the Transit Road cut across the slope of a hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. It cuts across the slope above Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that slope extend upwards as one moves approximately south?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. If one moves south, then it climbs up, up the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also gave evidence this morning that in mid-May, Grbavica was occupied, I think you said to the river. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you indicate that on the map in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What colour pen did you use to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I used a dark blue pen, marked it with a line which ends up in an arrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please point out that line.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've also given evidence that following the occupation, a headquarters was set up. Were you asked to mark the location of the headquarters on the map in 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think I marked it with an X, with a cross -- actually, this little square that looks more like a plus, sign for plus, which you can see on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please point to that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see beneath the square with what appears to be a plus in it, there appears to be a dot or a circle in blue ink?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you place that there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object at this point because my learned colleague wanted the witness to show a cross below Grbavica, but I must say that this was not handwritten by the witness. It is a part of a map, and I think that it stands for an emergency unit of some sort. I wish to avoid any misunderstanding. I will cross-examine the witness on this issue; however, I must point to the Court at this time that this is a Red Cross sign. It is not a sign that was put in by the witness. Because we also have an original, one could plainly see what is part of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I think the witness was asked to indicate a certain place, and whether it was written by himself on the map or whether it was red or green or blue. I don't think that this has to do anything with admissibility. And of course, you can cross-examine the witness on colours or meanings. But I think it's not appropriate that you give additional information to what has not been the testimony of the witness at this moment. So you can do that during cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the blue dot or circle indicate anything in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It seems to me that I made a mistake. I confused the two signs. It is the blue circle or a dot that indicated the headquarters that was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at about that time, that is, around May of 1992, was anything happening in terms of the local residents of Grbavica in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, can you tell us whether there was any recruiting in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, a mobilisation of all males from 18 up to 60 years of age was immediately carried out. And call-up papers were put up on visible places all around Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the conflict began, from your observation, what was the ethnic composition of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The ethnic composition was mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which groups lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. And other minorities to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the mobilisation apply to all or some of the ethnic groups who lived in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The mobilisation applied only to males of Serb ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to the other ethnic groups who lived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: If you're referring to the mobilisation, no. People from other ethnic groups were not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your observation, did the conflict at about that time, that is April, May of 1992, appear to impact in any way, either adversely or favourably upon the other ethnic groups, that is the non-Serb ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Of course it had major negative impact on other ethnic groups, non-Serb ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What impact, if any, did it have upon you and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We lived in fear, and we had good reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those reasons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We were exposed to the danger of being evicted or killed or mistreated either physically or psychologically at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to members of the Croatian community who you knew in that regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They were expelled, forced to perform forced labour. Women were sometimes raped. Those who were taken away never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any members of your immediate family live in Grbavica at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, my parents lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you consider your plight in relation to the danger of living in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I was aware of the danger that I was exposed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make a decision on a course of action so as to minimise that danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that decision?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: At one point I decided to report to the units of the Serb army, that is, to volunteer to join that army. I did this together with a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss that decision with your parents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did you think that enlisting would reduce the danger?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, I thought that the mere membership in that army would protect me from the assaults that I had -- that I previously mentioned, and that I would also be in a position not only to protect myself but also my parents. I apologise. I have to mention that I did want to leave Grbavica, to flee; however, my father flatly refused any such suggestion. And his idea was that I should leave if I wanted but that they would stay behind, which is something that I couldn't accept. I didn't want to leave them behind alone, because I was afraid what might happen to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that your father flatly refused any such suggestion, what was the suggestion that your father refused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, the suggestion that all three of us should, as soon as possible, leave Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having decided to enlist, how did you make contact with the military forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Me and my neighbour were taken to the headquarters by an individual. We had told him what we wanted to do, and he said that there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would be no problems, that he would take us there to report and that he would arrange for everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "headquarters," do you mean those at the position marked by the blue circle, or other headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I refer to the position that I previously indicated. I made a mistake. Before I said that the location in question was marked with a square with a plus in it, but on the other hand, it is actually the blue dot that indicates the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you attended the headquarters, who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Once we got there, this young man who took us there spoke to some people. Nobody asked us anything: who we were, what we wanted to do there. They were just happy that more people were joining them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what happened at the headquarters in relation to you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When the three of us arrived there, this young man explained to them that he had two volunteers who wanted to join the army. They checked some papers, some records, to see what platoon had the least number of people, so that we would be assigned there. Then they set about looking for a platoon commander who would later become my commander, [redacted] [redacted]. They managed to find him, and it was him to took us to an adjacent building across the street, which actually constituted business premises for the Digitron Buje company before the war, and that is where we were given weapons. After that we were informed that we should report to a review in the evening hours and that after that review we would be sent to positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report for the review in the evening hours, as requested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: After the review I was sent to the position in the vicinity of the Miljacka River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that position near any street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The name of the street was Lenjinova Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you arrived at that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: After we arrived at that position, we realised that it was a high-rise building consisting of 14 or 15 floors. There were actually four skyscrapers in that area, and me and my colleague were assigned to the third skyscraper, looking from the cultural hall, that is, from left to right. It was still daylight when we got there, and we stayed there throughout the night until the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where exactly in relation to the third skyscraper were you stationed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We were stationed in front of the skyscraper, at the entrance to the skyscraper, on that side, that is, on the side where the entrance to the skyscraper is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many floors did the skyscraper have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think it had 14 floors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that apply to each of the four skyscrapers in that area, that is, around 14 floors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All of them were the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what period of time was that your area of service, that is, in the vicinity of the four skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was there from the 22nd of June until the beginning of May, when I left Grbavica, but on six or seven occasions I spent five or six days at a different location. I was in position there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having regard to your earlier evidence, I take it that the 22nd of June, 1992, was the day that you enlisted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it would -- the answer would be more precise, the 22nd of June, and May. We don't know which year is in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the date that you enlisted, having regard to your earlier evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'll try to be more precise. The dates in question were the 22nd of June, 1992, until the beginning of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. You've told us that you were assigned to a platoon, and that you reported on the evening of the date that you enlisted to the area of the third skyscraper. What area did that platoon operate in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the question is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll approach it a different way. Approximately how many members were there to the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were between -- there was a varying number of members, but on average 25. Sometimes more, sometimes less. Some people would arrive, some would leave. But the average was 25.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were first assigned to the area around the third skyscraper, how many other members of the platoon, if any, were there with you with that area of control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: About 25 men. I can't give a precise figure. I don't remember exactly, but about 25 were present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By way of clarification, do you mean that there were 25 around the third skyscraper or over a broader area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me about the number of men in the platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were assigned to the third skyscraper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were only the two of us in the third skyscraper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there men assigned to each of the four skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, there were men from our platoon who had been assigned to all four skyscrapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many to each skyscraper approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were about -- there were three men in the first skyscraper. There were two in the second one. There were two in the third one. And there were four in the fourth skyscraper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware as to whether the responsibilities for the platoon extended into the interior of the skyscrapers or just the grounds surrounding them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We were deployed at that line in order to defend that line. So I want to say to defend that line of defence from any possible attacks, from whatever direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that involve members of your platoon entering and going up into any of the four skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, but very rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other buildings apart from the four skyscrapers which were within the area of responsibility of your platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The primary school, Borisa Kovacevic; and the pioneer centre, Bosko Buha [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many members of the platoon were stationed at each of those three sites?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There was a varying number, but usually there were about four men in the school, four in the nursery, and four in the pioneer centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the commander of your platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [redacted] was the name of the commander of my platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he remain the commander throughout the time of your membership of that platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He didn't. He was only the commander for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately when was he replaced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Sometime in the winter, I think. The first following winter, the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him after he left, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. He became deputy commander of a battalion in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced him as the platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When I first arrived at the position, he was replaced by [redacted]. And this replacement took place when I first arrived at the position. And I can't remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What period of time was he platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [redacted] is his name. I remember his surname. He was there for a very short period of time. And he later on died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [redacted] replaced him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he your commander, that is, the platoon commander, for the duration of the time that you stayed in the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, while I was there, he was the platoon commander all that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, when was it that you left the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I left at the beginning of May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, coming back to the headquarters where you enlisted, how many -- I'll withdraw that. Above a platoon by way of military structure, is there a company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many platoons were there in your company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think there were three platoons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that the headquarters were company headquarters. How many companies were there which -- for which that place was the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were two companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your company commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Dragan Maletic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Up until the winter, the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He also was transferred to the battalion headquarters, and he had some sort of duties -- some sort of operative duties there. He was responsible for operative activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where those battalion headquarters were located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I do. In Banja Luka Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier you said that the first commander of your platoon became deputy commander of the battalion. Did you mean, in relation to him, deputy commander of the battalion with its headquarters at Banja Luka Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure that it had a particular name. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said that your commander became deputy commander of -- withdraw that. When you said that your company commander later became deputy commander of the battalion, did you mean by that the commander which was above your company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So having regard to your evidence, both your first platoon commander and a later company commander were promoted to a battalion level during your time in the platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion was Stojanovic at the beginning, and then he was followed by Commander Aleksandar Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the commanders above the battalion level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I know the name of a certain officer whom they often mentioned. His surname was Milosevic. I don't know what rank he held or what duties he performed, but they often spoke about him in conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the time of your enlistment. You've told us that you had done military service at an earlier point in your life. Did that military service result in any documentation that you possessed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I had a military service booklet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you produce that at the time that you enlisted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. We had to provide that military service booklet to the headquarters that we spoke about earlier on in Grbavica. A few days later, this booklet was returned to us and we were allowed to hold onto it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown a booklet and some accompanying papers. I indicate that this is the original of Exhibit number P289. Exhibit P289 is, in effect, a photocopy of the booklet that the witness is to be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I remind you that we would talk about documents as long as they were not yet admitted into evidence, and that you would also indicate whether you intend to tender the document into evidence or not or just have it marked for identification. I assume that you want to tender into this evidence this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just the photocopy, Mr. President, not the original. I simply want the witness to identify the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you again, Mr. Ierace, be very careful as far as showing any part of this evidence on the ELMO is concerned, for obvious reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have that in mind. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the booklet that you have been shown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I can recognise it. It's my booklet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of booklet is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It's a military booklet, a military service booklet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the booklet that you handed over when you enlisted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that it was returned to you a few days later. When it was returned, was there anything added to the booklet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think that it was stamped. Some sort of stamp had been added, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. designating a military post to which my unit belonged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please indicate the page or pages on which these stamps were added.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It's on page 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that your name does not appear on the entry on that page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, it's not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, would you please read, firstly, the handwritten words which were entered on that page.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Military post, 7.536, Han Pijesak, the 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what "Han Pijesak" refers to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent sure, but I think the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was located there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there's also a stamp which appears over that wording. Would you please read the words which appear on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It says "Military post, 7.536, Han Pijesak."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that. Now, with the booklet, I think there are some sheets of paper. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise those pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does each of them have a date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, there are dates on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please go to the piece of paper which has the earliest date. Well, firstly, how many pieces of paper are there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Three pieces of paper here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please go to the piece of paper which has the earliest date and tell us essentially what it is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It's an authorisation. It's a grant for absence of leave [as interpreted]. Authorisation is granted to the soldier from the 10th of October until the 18th of October, 1992. His leave shall be taken advantage of in Sombor, and it also says that there is also a line where the battalion commander can sign. It's been signed and there is a stamp. The authorisation was issued on the 9th of October, 1992. The number is 1.530 through 92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the soldier that it relates to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It relates to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. So that's leave -- I take it from what you have said, it's a leave authorisation in respect of yourself. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the interests of saving time, do either of the other two slips of paper -- are either of the other two slips of paper authorisations of leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. And the next smaller piece of paper is also authorisation for leave of absence, and the third paper relates to another authorisation granting me -- granting authorisation to cross the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both of those further authorisations relate to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the relevant dates for the second leave authorisation in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: From the 10th of May to the 18th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Sorry. The date on which authorisation was granted is the 8th of May 1993. It has also been signed by the command, by the battalion command in Banja Luka Street. The deputy commander signed it. This authorisation was signed in my presence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the third slip of paper relate to a different period of leave or the same period as one of the other two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As I said, it relates to a different period of leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that completes the questions I seek to ask in relation to the booklet and the slips of paper. As I earlier indicated, I will be tendering the photocopies of those documents. In the meantime, might the originals be returned. I would also ask that the witness be shown again the map which was earlier described as Map 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before we start to cover a new issue, Mr. Ierace, would this be a suitable time to have a short break? And may I also remind you that you are a little bit over 50 percent of time indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in relation to that, I appreciate that there was a two-hour estimate on this witness. I anticipate that it may take longer than two hours to get through the essential evidence in chief. I've already moved -- I've already reached the point where I will not lead from this witness any of the detailed history of the pre-indictment period. I seek the understanding of the Trial Chamber and seek that I be granted some additional time, if needed, to complete the essential evidence in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea yet on how much time you would need, or extra time?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would have a better idea towards the end of the two hours, but I anticipate at this stage it will probably be an additional hour. It may not be that long; it may be a little longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll consider your request. We'll then adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to be informed by the parties about the differences of names on the list. Has it been sorted out yet or not? Not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please both provide me again with the list just for one second. Mr. Usher, if you would please again bring -- yes, please. Defence also. Yes, please. I would like to have the lists. Yes, I'll do it in Dutch. I can't give you a solution. I don't know -- is there any specific reason why the parties could not solve this problem during a half-hour break or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There isn't, Mr. President. There is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's leave it just -- if there's no reason to be explained, unless Mr. Piletta-Zanin has any -- if there's no reason, I'll just inform you that when I specifically ask you to do something over the break -- because I checked all the details about witness case as far as I could find them, and I'm a bit surprised that the parties did not follow the instructions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence took advantage of the break to have a meeting with General Galic, which seemed to be urgent and essential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is why.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise. I can inform the Trial Chamber that on Friday I spoke to my learned friend Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and we have arranged to meet after court this afternoon, that is, after we finish in the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it would be possible to spend five minutes of the lunch break on this issue so that we would be informed this afternoon, and then perhaps have a longer meeting. I think five minutes would be possible. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is with pleasure that the Defence will accord that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We then will continue the cross-examination of -- the examination-in-chief of Witness D.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when did you cease to be a member of the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: At the beginning of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I went on leave and did not return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I did not return because I was afraid for my life. I was afraid I'd be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you fear would kill you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was afraid I would be killed in battle, in the conflicts, and I wanted to join up with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some more questions now about the chain of command. You've told us the names of your platoon commander and company commander and something of the structure. When you received orders from time to time, who gave you those orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We received orders from the leaders of the companies and platoons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way did you receive those orders? For instance, were they written or were they given to you orally or were they passed to you by other people, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We received oral orders, and usually those orders were given during the evening reviews, and also in the mornings, before we left to take up our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts were the morning meetings held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They were also held at the headquarters, which are marked on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the evening reviews conducted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: At those same headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Typically, who would attend those two types of meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The leader of the platoon and the leader of the company. Sometimes the leader of the company was absent, but the platoon leader was always present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the other members of the platoon itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Who do you mean when you say "other members of the platoon"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your fellow soldiers in the platoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They would also attend the reviews. Let me be clearer: Before taking up our positions, we would attend the reviews, which means that if we had a daily shift, we would go to the headquarters for review. Or if it was an evening shift, we would go to the headquarters once again first, and then go to take up our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were the shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: About 10 minutes, maybe 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What period of time were you on duty per day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The shifts and shift schedules differed, but usually it meant a 12-hour shift, and then we would have 24 hours off. But sometimes we would be off for only 12 hours, unless we were at Grbavica and other positions. And we would be on those positions for five or six days at a go sometimes, which means that we didn't attend the reviews but we would stay in our positions throughout at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you living whilst you were a member of the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First of all, I lived in my own house. And then later on, I lived in my parents' apartment together with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back to the issue of commander control, in between the morning and evening briefings, did you have any means of communication to your platoon commander, that is, when you were in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We did have the possibility of communicating with the headquarters. We had a telephone link. But let me mention that it was a military telephone link, not a civilian line. It was a special telephone communications line set up for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Typically, where was your platoon commander when you were on duty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: He was usually at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the morning and evening meetings, were you and your fellow soldiers able to raise any matters if you wished with your commanders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any impression as to where the orders that you received from your commanders originated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was my impression that those orders came from the battalion command in Banja Luka Street. And I can support that, substantiate it, by some things that I personally heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those things and who said them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: This refers to conversations with platoon or company leaders, and with respect to our deployment to other positions. None of us liked to take up those new positions, and we tried to solve the problem. We wanted to avoid going. But we were always told that the problem would be brought up for discussion at the headquarters, but that there was little likelihood of the decision being in my favour. If there were any other problems that they weren't able to give an answer to, they promised that they would ask at the meetings in the battalion headquarters and try to solve the problem that had arisen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were told that the problem would be brought up for discussion at the headquarters, and you were told that by your platoon and company leaders. Which headquarters were they referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: You could only have a discussion up to a certain point, but the headquarters they meant was the battalion headquarters in Banja Luka Street. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you commenced as a member of the platoon, were you given orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We received orders that we had to be at our positions where we had been deployed and that we should not leave our positions. Those were strict orders. And also, orders with respect to when we were to open fire or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Which orders do you mean of the ones that I mentioned?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The orders with respect to when you were to open fire or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The orders were that we could open fire freely. That's what was literally said. They told us that we could shoot at anything that moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who first gave you that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The platoon commander. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any orders as to whom you were to fire upon from your company commander at any stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. He issued orders with respect to firing, and the orders were - let me repeat once again - that we could fire at anything and everything that moved, and anything we thought might jeopardise our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you received those orders from your platoon and company commander, was any distinction drawn between civilians and combatants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, no distinction of that kind was ever drawn. Nobody ever said that we should fire at something or not fire at something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive orders during your time in the platoon from any of your commanders to the effect that you were not to fire upon civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I never received any order to that effect expressly stated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in the platoon -- withdraw that. When you joined the platoon, were you provided with a firearm or firearms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I received a rifle, a semi-automatic rifle, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What calibre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: 7.62 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in the platoon, did you ever fire your firearm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Typically, what were the circumstances when you discharged your firearm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: For example, in circumstances when something in the dark would rustle in the bushes and I thought there was somebody moving around, in situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might the witness be shown Map 1. That is the map he had earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm about to ask the witness to place some further markings on the map. Mr. President, do you have a preference as to the colour of the pen that the witness should use? I should indicate that it already has some black and blue markings on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Blue is the colour of the Defence as far as I remember. Black was the colour of the Prosecution. If it would be possible to use a thick marker perhaps and still stay with black, and later on have the thick marker be used also for the Defence if any additional markings are required. Are there any thick markers? Because what's on the map now is all rather thin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think we have a thick black marker here, but perhaps the witness could place a number of black marks rather than one single one so as to emphasise the thickness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there no thick markers around, Madam Registrar? We found a thick black marker to start with. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, the Defence would like to stress that it considers it would be more useful if the witness were shown the empty map that we used and the one we decided to use for each witness depending on the markings they would make, especially, as I said, this is only a section of town. It's not a whole map. It just shows a section of town. I don't know how relevant it will be for this witness to mark in the positions on this section map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the difference might be that this map is far more detailed than the big black-and-white map we used. So if the Prosecution needs this detail, then I think -- what we also could do is to have this -- is there any extra copies, so that we have the pre-marked map as the first exhibit and then the at-the-trial-marked map as a second exhibit to be tendered into evidence, so that there will be no misunderstanding? So the blank map would then be the pre-marked blank map. Do we have any extra copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I took some steps to try to obtain a blank copy for that reason, and one was not available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't mind if you use the pre-marked copy, but if these are two exhibits, then, of course, it is clear what is the pre-marked one and what has been added on the second one. So I wouldn't mind you to use this map, but an extra copy tendered separately into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that case I -- excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in that case, I'll take a different course. I had intended to avoid tendering unnecessarily a number of maps. I ask that the witness be shown Map 3 of the same exhibit number, and that will necessitate a further sticker being placed over the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you then have him make markings on it, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. On reflection, Mr. President, perhaps the witness should be given a second copy of Map 1, because there are some additional markings to be made. I hand up an additional copy of Map 1, which has the witness's name removed, and perhaps we should call this Map 1A so as to distinguish it from the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think for the Registry it's easier if it gets a specific exhibit number, and there will be a sticker put on it later on. And since there's a distinctive number, it must be clear enough. So now an additional copy of the first page of what has been introduced earlier as -- if you just allow me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if you use another copy, please keep together all five pages, because exhibits -- well, still documents, but soon to be Exhibit 3637, consist of five pages. So if we have the copy that will be used by the witness later marked as Exhibit 3637D, for Witness D, then it should also consist of five pages, because that's -- otherwise we have to give it new numbers, et cetera. So if you please have a copy of the pre-marked map similar as the one that has been shown before to the witness. Markings can be made on that map, and it later will get number 3637D. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence accepts that it be this map, but not parts of the map, because I think for the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Trial Chamber, it would be more useful if we had all the positions marked in this one map which the witness has marked in the five copies of sections of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said five -- it should be five pages. So all the pages indicating it's Map 1, 2 -- Map 1, Map 2, Map 3, Map 4, Map 5. So all the five can now be presented to the witness. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I take this opportunity to say that if Defence should ask questions during its cross-examination concerning other portions of the map, it is going to be very difficult, because we do not have an entire map. It would be very useful for us to have the whole town depicted in a map. It would facilitate our work to a great extent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the objection -- if the Prosecution wants to provide this map to the witness with these details, then I think there's no reason not to admit it. Of course, you can come up with another map of the whole city, and whatever one you use, and cross-examine the witness on the subjects covered by the examination-in-chief. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please go to Map 3. Sir, do you see on Map 3 a blue line alongside the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the markings on this map as having been made by you in February of 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please explain to the Trial Chamber the significance of the blue line on that map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The blue line indicates one part of the positions on the Miljacka River, where my platoon was deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, would you please point to that blue line which is on the display at the moment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, whilst you were stationed in that position during those times, did you see any other members of the military enter those buildings, that is, persons other than members of your platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Occasionally some individuals who were members of the army but not members of my platoon would come to those buildings; however, not very often. I apologise. I'm sorry. I just want to say that what I just said refers to the period of time while we were there, because after our shift, other platoons would be deployed to the same area. So I'm talking about my shift. During our presence there, from time to time soldiers belonging to other units would visit those positions. When we were not there, other soldiers, that is, members of other platoons, were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the soldiers who entered the buildings had any particular skills?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Soldiers who were assigned to sniper activity would visit those skyscrapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any such soldiers in your platoon, that is, soldiers assigned to sniper activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, not from our platoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any such soldiers assigned to your company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The soldiers who were in charge of sniper activity were not directly members of our company, but they would always go to the headquarters that I indicated earlier on and would go to those positions at the same time we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to headquarters, do you mean the company headquarters or the battalion headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm referring to the company headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you to mean that each morning, members of the sniping unit would accompany your platoon to the skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where you were positioned, that is, on the -- at the ground level around the skyscrapers, did you from time to time hear the sound of any firearms emanating from the upper levels of the skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that sound very often. They were actually never down there where we were on ground level positions but upstairs. But I don't know exactly which floors they occupied. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with any members of the sniper unit that was operating from the skyscrapers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Very often we had opportunity to talk to them, sometimes when they were going to the skyscraper or leaving the skyscraper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever discuss the nature of their targets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They would usually say that they had hit someone. However, I was never sure whether they had actually hit someone or whether it was merely their intention to leave such an impression on us. I'm not sure that they had indeed hit someone every time they said that. Sometimes I had the impression that they merely wanted to say that they had had a very successful day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that they attended the same briefing meetings as you. Did you ever hear them receive any separate orders from those that were given to you and the other soldiers in the platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was my impression that they received orders from the battalion headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that from time to time, you were stationed at a different section. Whereabouts was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was referring to the area which I had marked with a blue line on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which map is that? Which number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Map Number 3. Map Number 3. What I want to say was that I was occasionally stationed at the first, second, and then the third skyscraper, or the fourth one. Sometimes I was at the position which was referred to as Obdanesta [phoen], a kindergarten, or pioneer's house. But most often I was deployed at the first skyscraper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also told us on a number of occasions you were moved to a quite different area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Those positions were in Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see those positions on the map to your right, that is, the positions in Ozrenska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
